title: Push Notification System Design · Staff Interview Lab

Transactional outbox.markdown: Notification intent and an outbox event commit in one local transaction. A relay dispatches later; replay can require idempotent consumers.

Fan-out.markdown: Expand one logical notification into recipient delivery jobs. Eager expansion pays work early; deferred expansion needs a later trigger.

Idempotency.markdown: Replaying the same logical request preserves its intended effect. Always specify the key, retention interval, and side-effect boundary.

Backpressure.markdown: Bound admitted work to protect downstream resources. Delayed retries and in-flight work still consume outstanding capacity.

Dead letter.markdown: Terminal work isolated for inspection or deliberate recovery after a permanent error or exhausted retry budget.

Kafka.markdown: A partitioned retained event log. Producers append records; consumers track positions. Consuming a record does not remove it. In this architecture, intent-events feeds Flink and delivery-jobs feeds push workers. The lab aggregates partitions and omits retention expiry.

Flink.markdown: A stream processing job. Here its boundary starts at KafkaSource, transforms an intent into recipient jobs in the fan-out operator, and ends at KafkaSink. Delivery workers and remote push gateways are outside Flink. Production recovery depends on checkpoint and connector configuration; those mechanisms are not simulated.

CDC relay.markdown: Change data capture or an outbox poller publishes committed database events to the broker. The model combines publish and acknowledgment in one relay tick; production must handle crash windows, replays, and database change positions.

Sender / source.markdown: The entity that publishes an event, such as a user, channel, or organization. Intent records carry this identity so audience resolution can query its followers.

Follower subscriptions.markdown: A relation from followed source identity to recipient identity. It determines the audience; the query limit bounds selected rows without creating users.

scenes.title: Accepted Is a Durable Promise
scenes.description: Follow one notification from an atomic database commit to distinct provider and device evidence.
scenes.markdown:
# Accepted Is a Durable Promise

## Architecture and ownership

The default **Architecture** view shows one concrete deployment. **Blue Kafka** owns two retained topic logs: intent-events and delivery-jobs. **Purple Flink** starts at KafkaSource, expands recipients in the fan-out operator, and ends at KafkaSink. Delivery workers, the retry timer, completion ledger, APNs/FCM, and devices are outside that job. Cylindrical pipes connect named ports across service boundaries; colored pipes mark transitions at the current tick. Nested blocks separate Kafka topic ownership from Flink processing stages. The topic blocks embed existing array objects in their local coordinates. Use **Records** to inspect the actual identities and consumer backlog.

Node status values show notification rows (DB), relayed intents (CDC), retained topic records (Kafka), intents awaiting processing (Flink header), consumed intents (KafkaSource), processing responsibilities (operator/sink), in-flight claims (workers), acceptance/receipt events, or live entries in support stores. The Kafka header marks ownership of both retained logs. Embedded arrays show the first three records; use Records for the full bounded projection. The Dead letters node counts stored permanent failures and exhausted retries. The separate Terminal dashboard also counts abandoned attempts.

Retries publish another delivery record; they do not delete earlier Kafka history. Deferred readers live in a separate read inbox and re-enter fan-out at tick 12. The ledger is checked before sending and records acknowledged completion; a lost provider acknowledgment leaves an uncertain effect.

Flink is a deployment choice for stateful, partitioned fan-out; simpler fan-out workers can implement the same contract. This simulation aggregates topics and consumer positions. It does **not** simulate partitions, checkpoints, consumer crashes, Kafka transactions, or Flink recovery. Kafka-to-Flink-to-Kafka exactly-once processing depends on checkpoint and connector configuration; it does not make a remote APNs/FCM effect exactly once. See [Kafka log and consumer design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/) and [Flink connector guarantees](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/connectors/datastream/guarantees/).

## Follow the current transition

The caption beneath the player explains **this tick**, including which structures changed and why. Use the small execution arrows beside the tick slider to move one scheduling round; the larger lesson arrows move between Predict, Execute, and Defend. Parameter changes recompute the trace from tick 0.

A useful Staff interview starts with a contract: **accepting the request means durable work exists**, not that a phone has displayed it. Begin with the two blue structures. At tick 1, the notification database contains n1 and the transactional outbox contains its dispatch intent. They belong to one local transaction.

## Worked default trace

With four recipients, two worker slots, and two gateway attempts per tick, tick 2 relays the outbox record into Kafka intent-events. At tick 3 the ready queue contains n1:u1 through n1:u4. Tick 4 claims the first two jobs. At tick 5 their gateway acceptances appear while the other two jobs are claimed. Tick 6 records the first two device receipts and the next two gateway acceptances. All four distinct receipts exist at tick 7.

The database is durable history; queue and worker arrays are live scheduling state; gateway and device arrays are histories. Repeated appearances of one ID are meaningful. Do not add their lengths together as if every appearance were a different user.

## Predict, then test

Before choosing **Lost first acceptance ACK**, predict whether a repeat send is possible even when dedupe is enabled. Run through ticks 5–9. The first gateway acceptance can occur without its completion acknowledgment being stored; a retry may therefore repeat that external effect. The local completed-job ledger cannot prove completion it never learned about.

Discuss a crash after transaction commit but before relay: the outbox record gives a recovery source. That database crash is an architectural thought experiment, not an injected failure in this lab. Likewise, production relays need leases, retention, and replay-safe consumers.

## Defend the design

Separate the API response, database commit, broker acknowledgment, provider acceptance, and device receipt. State recovery ownership at each boundary and choose metrics for stuck outbox age, queue age, and terminal errors. The outbox fixes the **local dual-write problem**; it does not create an atomic transaction with a remote push provider.

The [AWS transactional outbox pattern](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/transactional-outbox.html) explains the local consistency problem and duplicate-message considerations. The lab is a deterministic teaching model, not an implementation of AWS or a push provider.

## Lab controls
Use the execution player to **step, play, rewind, or scrub ticks 0–24**. Changing a parameter recomputes the entire run from tick 0; it does not inject a new event at the current tick. The failure selector chooses a reproducible failure schedule. Each tick is a simulation scheduling round, not a measured second.

Cells carry logical IDs such as `n1:u1`; the same ID can appear in history and live state. Database and outbox cells are notification IDs, while delivery cells identify notification/recipient pairs. Each recipient has one modeled device. Arrays are projections of records, not a suggested database schema. A `+N more` cell summarizes additional entries; counters retain exact totals. Empty structures show ∅. The amber cell rim indicates an array position changed; it is not a guarantee of animated identity across services.

Commit occurs at tick 1, relay at 2, expansion at 3, worker claim at 4, provider response at 5, and earliest device receipt at 6. Worker slots and gateway attempts per tick independently constrain dispatch. Retry delays are deterministic exponential backoff, capped at three attempts. Failure 4 keeps the provider unavailable through tick 24, exposing retry exhaustion and dead letters. Production needs jitter, Retry-After handling, durable leases, and observability. Device receipt is modeled evidence; display and opening are outside this model.

The dedupe ledger suppresses **known completed replays**; it cannot remove uncertainty after a remote acceptance with a lost acknowledgment. At-most-once refuses retries and can lose work. The bounded at-least-once policy retries transient failures but can end in a dead letter; it does not promise eventual device delivery.


**Records view:** inspect DB → outbox → Kafka intent-events → Flink input → Kafka delivery-jobs → worker consumer backlog → workers → gateway → device, followed by retry, completion, terminal, and deferred state. Kafka topic logs retain records after consumption; the worker backlog shrinks when claims advance the consumer position. Gateway/device histories include repeated attempts; the receipt counter counts distinct recipients.

The dashboard cells are exact counters: Gateway counts acceptance events, Receipts counts distinct modeled recipient receipts, Duplicates counts repeated gateway acceptance, Writes counts the illustrative commit/materialization operations, and Terminal counts permanent failures, exhausted retries, or abandoned uncertain attempts.


## Sender and audience resolution

Each intent carries a notification identity and a sender/source identity. A sender can be a publisher, channel, organization, or user. The follower subscriptions table links a known recipient to a followed source. Fan-out queries that relation, joins the recipient directory, deduplicates targets, and applies the **Follower query limit** before expanding delivery jobs. The source directory and recipient directory are explicit modeled records, not live personal data. Change **Sender / followed source**: publisher-1 has 40 followers, while channel-2 has u2, u4, u6, and u8. A limit of three selects u1/u2/u3 for publisher-1 and u2/u4/u6 for channel-2. The limit never invents a recipient.

The two lookup arrows show query and result, distinct from deferred-work arrows. Lookup is synchronous within the fan-out tick; lookup latency, pagination, subscription changes, privacy rules, and device-token lookup are not simulated. Admission preflights this fixed subscription snapshot to reserve exact target obligations. Production must choose an audience snapshot and handle changes between admission and processing. Deferred readers contains already resolved recipients; it is not the subscription directory. Use Records for source identities, selected subscription links, and resolved request-to-recipient pairs.


## Inspect the scenario data

The data section contains ordinary tables: settings (one row of scalar options), submissions (tick/count rows), sources and targets (identity rows), memberships (source/target rows), replays (tick/request/target rows), and receiptExclusions (target rows). There is no serialized model cell. dataTable(name) supplies a whole table; dataTable(name,row,column) still reads one cell. The domain combines these structured inputs at evaluation time. Edit a subscription row to change who follows a source.
scenes.prompt: Teach durability boundaries before throughput. Ask the learner to name what each acknowledgment proves. The outbox model commits atomically; there is no database-crash control. Lost ACK is the remote send acknowledgment. Never equate gateway acceptance with device display. Explain concrete boundaries: Kafka owns retained topic logs; Flink contains KafkaSource, fan-out operator, and KafkaSink. Delivery workers and external APNs/FCM are outside Flink. Use Architecture for ownership and Records for identities. Checkpoints, partitions, and transactional connector guarantees are production discussion, not simulated features. Explain that intents contain sender/source identity, which may identify a channel rather than a user. Followers are selected from explicit subscriptions and a known target directory. The recipients slider is a query limit, not synthetic user creation. Do not claim lookup latency or live user data are modeled.

scenes.title: Fan-out on Write: One Intent, Many Jobs
scenes.description: Materialize recipient work early and observe how fan-out amplifies downstream scheduling.
scenes.markdown:
# Fan-out on Write: One Intent, Many Jobs

## Architecture and ownership

The default **Architecture** view shows one concrete deployment. **Blue Kafka** owns two retained topic logs: intent-events and delivery-jobs. **Purple Flink** starts at KafkaSource, expands recipients in the fan-out operator, and ends at KafkaSink. Delivery workers, the retry timer, completion ledger, APNs/FCM, and devices are outside that job. Cylindrical pipes connect named ports across service boundaries; colored pipes mark transitions at the current tick. Nested blocks separate Kafka topic ownership from Flink processing stages. The topic blocks embed existing array objects in their local coordinates. Use **Records** to inspect the actual identities and consumer backlog.

Node status values show notification rows (DB), relayed intents (CDC), retained topic records (Kafka), intents awaiting processing (Flink header), consumed intents (KafkaSource), processing responsibilities (operator/sink), in-flight claims (workers), acceptance/receipt events, or live entries in support stores. The Kafka header marks ownership of both retained logs. Embedded arrays show the first three records; use Records for the full bounded projection. The Dead letters node counts stored permanent failures and exhausted retries. The separate Terminal dashboard also counts abandoned attempts.

Retries publish another delivery record; they do not delete earlier Kafka history. Deferred readers live in a separate read inbox and re-enter fan-out at tick 12. The ledger is checked before sending and records acknowledged completion; a lost provider acknowledgment leaves an uncertain effect.

Flink is a deployment choice for stateful, partitioned fan-out; simpler fan-out workers can implement the same contract. This simulation aggregates topics and consumer positions. It does **not** simulate partitions, checkpoints, consumer crashes, Kafka transactions, or Flink recovery. Kafka-to-Flink-to-Kafka exactly-once processing depends on checkpoint and connector configuration; it does not make a remote APNs/FCM effect exactly once. See [Kafka log and consumer design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/) and [Flink connector guarantees](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/connectors/datastream/guarantees/).

## Follow the current transition

The caption beneath the player explains **this tick**, including which structures changed and why. Use the small execution arrows beside the tick slider to move one scheduling round; the larger lesson arrows move between Predict, Execute, and Defend. Parameter changes recompute the trace from tick 0.

A notification API call is not a unit of downstream load. One accepted logical notification may create a recipient job for every follower or subscribed device. This scenario materializes all recipients immediately after relay, even if some users would not otherwise read the notification.

## Worked default trace

One notification commits at tick 1 for eight recipients. Relay runs at tick 2; tick 3 creates eight ready jobs. Two worker slots claim n1:u1 and n1:u2 at tick 4. They are accepted at tick 5, and their receipts appear at tick 6. The remaining pairs follow the same schedule: four dispatch rounds complete all eight distinct receipts at tick 9.

Observe that the database still contains one notification while recipient structures contain eight jobs. The toy write counter, when inspected through the domain, counts two commit writes plus eight eager materializations: ten modeled writes. This is illustrative accounting, not database write units, index costs, replication, or provider billing.

## Predict, then test

Reduce **Recipients per notification** from eight to two. Predict the ready queue at tick 3 and the completion tick before running. Expect two jobs and all receipts at tick 6. Restore eight recipients, increase workers and gateway rate together to four, and predict two dispatch rounds with completion at tick 7. Increasing workers alone plateaus when the gateway rate stays two: dispatch is paced by the smaller limit. Worker concurrency and downstream quota are different resources.

Capacity is an admission control only in the later backpressure scenario. It does not bound this scene's ready queue.

## Defend the design

Eager fan-out makes recipient work available early and supports per-recipient tracking. Its costs include write amplification, broadcast spikes, and work for inactive users. A Staff answer identifies audience-size distributions, freshness requirements, recipient eligibility snapshots, token churn, and hot partition risk before choosing a policy.

A hybrid design can eagerly serve ordinary audiences and defer large broadcasts. Batching, segmentation, and hybrid switching are discussion extensions, not controls implemented here. Avoid presenting provider topic messaging as identical to your own recipient queue.

[FCM scaling guidance](https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging/scale-fcm) discusses quota pressure, traffic spikes, and smoothing requests. Use the observed recipient expansion to explain why ingress request rate alone understates provider demand.

## Lab controls
Use the execution player to **step, play, rewind, or scrub ticks 0–24**. Changing a parameter recomputes the entire run from tick 0; it does not inject a new event at the current tick. The failure selector chooses a reproducible failure schedule. Each tick is a simulation scheduling round, not a measured second.

Cells carry logical IDs such as `n1:u1`; the same ID can appear in history and live state. Database and outbox cells are notification IDs, while delivery cells identify notification/recipient pairs. Each recipient has one modeled device. Arrays are projections of records, not a suggested database schema. A `+N more` cell summarizes additional entries; counters retain exact totals. Empty structures show ∅. The amber cell rim indicates an array position changed; it is not a guarantee of animated identity across services.

Commit occurs at tick 1, relay at 2, expansion at 3, worker claim at 4, provider response at 5, and earliest device receipt at 6. Worker slots and gateway attempts per tick independently constrain dispatch. Retry delays are deterministic exponential backoff, capped at three attempts. Failure 4 keeps the provider unavailable through tick 24, exposing retry exhaustion and dead letters. Production needs jitter, Retry-After handling, durable leases, and observability. Device receipt is modeled evidence; display and opening are outside this model.

The dedupe ledger suppresses **known completed replays**; it cannot remove uncertainty after a remote acceptance with a lost acknowledgment. At-most-once refuses retries and can lose work. The bounded at-least-once policy retries transient failures but can end in a dead letter; it does not promise eventual device delivery.


**Records view:** inspect DB → outbox → Kafka intent-events → Flink input → Kafka delivery-jobs → worker consumer backlog → workers → gateway → device, followed by retry, completion, terminal, and deferred state. Kafka topic logs retain records after consumption; the worker backlog shrinks when claims advance the consumer position. Gateway/device histories include repeated attempts; the receipt counter counts distinct recipients.

The dashboard cells are exact counters: Gateway counts acceptance events, Receipts counts distinct modeled recipient receipts, Duplicates counts repeated gateway acceptance, Writes counts the illustrative commit/materialization operations, and Terminal counts permanent failures, exhausted retries, or abandoned uncertain attempts.


## Sender and audience resolution

Each intent carries a notification identity and a sender/source identity. A sender can be a publisher, channel, organization, or user. The follower subscriptions table links a known recipient to a followed source. Fan-out queries that relation, joins the recipient directory, deduplicates targets, and applies the **Follower query limit** before expanding delivery jobs. The source directory and recipient directory are explicit modeled records, not live personal data. Change **Sender / followed source**: publisher-1 has 40 followers, while channel-2 has u2, u4, u6, and u8. A limit of three selects u1/u2/u3 for publisher-1 and u2/u4/u6 for channel-2. The limit never invents a recipient.

The two lookup arrows show query and result, distinct from deferred-work arrows. Lookup is synchronous within the fan-out tick; lookup latency, pagination, subscription changes, privacy rules, and device-token lookup are not simulated. Admission preflights this fixed subscription snapshot to reserve exact target obligations. Production must choose an audience snapshot and handle changes between admission and processing. Deferred readers contains already resolved recipients; it is not the subscription directory. Use Records for source identities, selected subscription links, and resolved request-to-recipient pairs.


## Inspect the scenario data

The data section contains ordinary tables: settings (one row of scalar options), submissions (tick/count rows), sources and targets (identity rows), memberships (source/target rows), replays (tick/request/target rows), and receiptExclusions (target rows). There is no serialized model cell. dataTable(name) supplies a whole table; dataTable(name,row,column) still reads one cell. The domain combines these structured inputs at evaluation time. Edit a subscription row to change who follows a source.
scenes.prompt: Keep notification count distinct from recipient intents. Default one notification creates eight jobs at tick3, all receipts tick9. Capacity slider has no effect here. Discuss celebrity/hybrid designs as extensions rather than simulated controls. Explain concrete boundaries: Kafka owns retained topic logs; Flink contains KafkaSource, fan-out operator, and KafkaSink. Delivery workers and external APNs/FCM are outside Flink. Use Architecture for ownership and Records for identities. Checkpoints, partitions, and transactional connector guarantees are production discussion, not simulated features. Explain that intents contain sender/source identity, which may identify a channel rather than a user. Followers are selected from explicit subscriptions and a known target directory. The recipients slider is a query limit, not synthetic user creation. Do not claim lookup latency or live user data are modeled.

scenes.title: Fan-out on Read: Deferred Work Has a Trigger
scenes.description: Observe early active recipients and later reconnecting recipients without promising a push to dormant clients.
scenes.markdown:
# Fan-out on Read: Deferred Work Has a Trigger

## Architecture and ownership

The default **Architecture** view shows one concrete deployment. **Blue Kafka** owns two retained topic logs: intent-events and delivery-jobs. **Purple Flink** starts at KafkaSource, expands recipients in the fan-out operator, and ends at KafkaSink. Delivery workers, the retry timer, completion ledger, APNs/FCM, and devices are outside that job. Cylindrical pipes connect named ports across service boundaries; colored pipes mark transitions at the current tick. Nested blocks separate Kafka topic ownership from Flink processing stages. The topic blocks embed existing array objects in their local coordinates. Use **Records** to inspect the actual identities and consumer backlog.

Node status values show notification rows (DB), relayed intents (CDC), retained topic records (Kafka), intents awaiting processing (Flink header), consumed intents (KafkaSource), processing responsibilities (operator/sink), in-flight claims (workers), acceptance/receipt events, or live entries in support stores. The Kafka header marks ownership of both retained logs. Embedded arrays show the first three records; use Records for the full bounded projection. The Dead letters node counts stored permanent failures and exhausted retries. The separate Terminal dashboard also counts abandoned attempts.

Retries publish another delivery record; they do not delete earlier Kafka history. Deferred readers live in a separate read inbox and re-enter fan-out at tick 12. The ledger is checked before sending and records acknowledged completion; a lost provider acknowledgment leaves an uncertain effect.

Flink is a deployment choice for stateful, partitioned fan-out; simpler fan-out workers can implement the same contract. This simulation aggregates topics and consumer positions. It does **not** simulate partitions, checkpoints, consumer crashes, Kafka transactions, or Flink recovery. Kafka-to-Flink-to-Kafka exactly-once processing depends on checkpoint and connector configuration; it does not make a remote APNs/FCM effect exactly once. See [Kafka log and consumer design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/) and [Flink connector guarantees](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/connectors/datastream/guarantees/).

## Follow the current transition

The caption beneath the player explains **this tick**, including which structures changed and why. Use the small execution arrows beside the tick slider to move one scheduling round; the larger lesson arrows move between Predict, Execute, and Defend. Parameter changes recompute the trace from tick 0.

Deferring recipient expansion changes **when work happens**. It does not magically send a push to a dormant device. Here, the early active set is fixed at half the audience, rounded up. The rest read or reconnect at tick 12, explicitly triggering later materialization. There is no active-fraction or reconnect-time control.

## Worked default trace

One notification commits for eight recipients at tick 1. Relay at tick 2 publishes the notification intent to Kafka. At tick 3 Flink consumes it, places four recipients in the read inbox, and publishes four active recipient jobs to delivery-jobs. Two slots process those jobs in two rounds; their four distinct receipts finish at tick 7.

The other four IDs remain pending. At tick 12 the modeled read trigger moves them into the ready queue. Because dispatch runs before this read event in the scheduler, their first claims occur at tick 13, first gateway acceptances at tick 14, and first receipts at tick 15. All eight recipients have receipts at tick 16.

The pending array makes outstanding intent visible. A production shared-record design might avoid enumerating dormant recipient intents upfront; this bounded model still tracks them for inspectability. Its write metric counts two commit writes plus the jobs actually materialized: six writes before the later reads and ten after tick 12. Eager fan-out also totals ten; the early saving defers work rather than eliminating eventual work. This is not a production database cost estimate.

## Predict, then test

Compare tick 3 here with fan-out on write: four ready jobs versus eight. Predict the tick 10 receipt count: four here, eight in the previous healthy default. Set recipients to seven and verify four initially active recipients and three deferred ones. Increase worker count and gateway rate together, then separate faster service from the unchanged tick 12 read trigger.

## Defend the design

Eager fan-out pays before reads; deferred fan-out shifts cost and latency onto a later trigger. Ask about active-user fraction, freshness, shared-record retention, eligibility changes, and reconstructing unread state after reconnect. In an interview, describe hybrid selection and reconciliation explicitly; they are design discussion, not simulated policy switches.

A device that never reconnects has no read trigger here. Provider acceptance also cannot establish display. [FCM scaling guidance](https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging/scale-fcm) supports planning downstream request pressure; the choice between these fan-out patterns remains an application architecture decision.

## Lab controls
Use the execution player to **step, play, rewind, or scrub ticks 0–24**. Changing a parameter recomputes the entire run from tick 0; it does not inject a new event at the current tick. The failure selector chooses a reproducible failure schedule. Each tick is a simulation scheduling round, not a measured second.

Cells carry logical IDs such as `n1:u1`; the same ID can appear in history and live state. Database and outbox cells are notification IDs, while delivery cells identify notification/recipient pairs. Each recipient has one modeled device. Arrays are projections of records, not a suggested database schema. A `+N more` cell summarizes additional entries; counters retain exact totals. Empty structures show ∅. The amber cell rim indicates an array position changed; it is not a guarantee of animated identity across services.

Commit occurs at tick 1, relay at 2, expansion at 3, worker claim at 4, provider response at 5, and earliest device receipt at 6. Worker slots and gateway attempts per tick independently constrain dispatch. Retry delays are deterministic exponential backoff, capped at three attempts. Failure 4 keeps the provider unavailable through tick 24, exposing retry exhaustion and dead letters. Production needs jitter, Retry-After handling, durable leases, and observability. Device receipt is modeled evidence; display and opening are outside this model.

The dedupe ledger suppresses **known completed replays**; it cannot remove uncertainty after a remote acceptance with a lost acknowledgment. At-most-once refuses retries and can lose work. The bounded at-least-once policy retries transient failures but can end in a dead letter; it does not promise eventual device delivery.


**Records view:** inspect DB → outbox → Kafka intent-events → Flink input → Kafka delivery-jobs → worker consumer backlog → workers → gateway → device, followed by retry, completion, terminal, and deferred state. Kafka topic logs retain records after consumption; the worker backlog shrinks when claims advance the consumer position. Gateway/device histories include repeated attempts; the receipt counter counts distinct recipients.

The dashboard cells are exact counters: Gateway counts acceptance events, Receipts counts distinct modeled recipient receipts, Duplicates counts repeated gateway acceptance, Writes counts the illustrative commit/materialization operations, and Terminal counts permanent failures, exhausted retries, or abandoned uncertain attempts.


## Sender and audience resolution

Each intent carries a notification identity and a sender/source identity. A sender can be a publisher, channel, organization, or user. The follower subscriptions table links a known recipient to a followed source. Fan-out queries that relation, joins the recipient directory, deduplicates targets, and applies the **Follower query limit** before expanding delivery jobs. The source directory and recipient directory are explicit modeled records, not live personal data. Change **Sender / followed source**: publisher-1 has 40 followers, while channel-2 has u2, u4, u6, and u8. A limit of three selects u1/u2/u3 for publisher-1 and u2/u4/u6 for channel-2. The limit never invents a recipient.

The two lookup arrows show query and result, distinct from deferred-work arrows. Lookup is synchronous within the fan-out tick; lookup latency, pagination, subscription changes, privacy rules, and device-token lookup are not simulated. Admission preflights this fixed subscription snapshot to reserve exact target obligations. Production must choose an audience snapshot and handle changes between admission and processing. Deferred readers contains already resolved recipients; it is not the subscription directory. Use Records for source identities, selected subscription links, and resolved request-to-recipient pairs.


## Inspect the scenario data

The data section contains ordinary tables: settings (one row of scalar options), submissions (tick/count rows), sources and targets (identity rows), memberships (source/target rows), replays (tick/request/target rows), and receiptExclusions (target rows). There is no serialized model cell. dataTable(name) supplies a whole table; dataTable(name,row,column) still reads one cell. The domain combines these structured inputs at evaluation time. Edit a subscription row to change who follows a source.
scenes.prompt: The active fraction is fixed ceil(N/2), not configurable. Four default active recipients finish tick7; pending remaining recipients read at tick12 and finish tick16. Explain deferred intent accounting and lower early work without claiming full write saving. Capacity has no effect. Explain concrete boundaries: Kafka owns retained topic logs; Flink contains KafkaSource, fan-out operator, and KafkaSink. Delivery workers and external APNs/FCM are outside Flink. Use Architecture for ownership and Records for identities. Checkpoints, partitions, and transactional connector guarantees are production discussion, not simulated features. Explain that intents contain sender/source identity, which may identify a channel rather than a user. Followers are selected from explicit subscriptions and a known target directory. The recipients slider is a query limit, not synthetic user creation. Do not claim lookup latency or live user data are modeled.

scenes.title: Scale the Actual Bottleneck
scenes.description: Three simultaneous notifications amplify into twenty-four jobs; compare worker slots with gateway quota.
scenes.markdown:
# Scale the Actual Bottleneck

## Architecture and ownership

The default **Architecture** view shows one concrete deployment. **Blue Kafka** owns two retained topic logs: intent-events and delivery-jobs. **Purple Flink** starts at KafkaSource, expands recipients in the fan-out operator, and ends at KafkaSink. Delivery workers, the retry timer, completion ledger, APNs/FCM, and devices are outside that job. Cylindrical pipes connect named ports across service boundaries; colored pipes mark transitions at the current tick. Nested blocks separate Kafka topic ownership from Flink processing stages. The topic blocks embed existing array objects in their local coordinates. Use **Records** to inspect the actual identities and consumer backlog.

Node status values show notification rows (DB), relayed intents (CDC), retained topic records (Kafka), intents awaiting processing (Flink header), consumed intents (KafkaSource), processing responsibilities (operator/sink), in-flight claims (workers), acceptance/receipt events, or live entries in support stores. The Kafka header marks ownership of both retained logs. Embedded arrays show the first three records; use Records for the full bounded projection. The Dead letters node counts stored permanent failures and exhausted retries. The separate Terminal dashboard also counts abandoned attempts.

Retries publish another delivery record; they do not delete earlier Kafka history. Deferred readers live in a separate read inbox and re-enter fan-out at tick 12. The ledger is checked before sending and records acknowledged completion; a lost provider acknowledgment leaves an uncertain effect.

Flink is a deployment choice for stateful, partitioned fan-out; simpler fan-out workers can implement the same contract. This simulation aggregates topics and consumer positions. It does **not** simulate partitions, checkpoints, consumer crashes, Kafka transactions, or Flink recovery. Kafka-to-Flink-to-Kafka exactly-once processing depends on checkpoint and connector configuration; it does not make a remote APNs/FCM effect exactly once. See [Kafka log and consumer design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/) and [Flink connector guarantees](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/connectors/datastream/guarantees/).

## Follow the current transition

The caption beneath the player explains **this tick**, including which structures changed and why. Use the small execution arrows beside the tick slider to move one scheduling round; the larger lesson arrows move between Predict, Execute, and Defend. Parameter changes recompute the trace from tick 0.

A Staff design must distinguish ingress volume, fan-out amplification, worker concurrency, and provider limits. This scenario commits **three notifications at tick 1**. With eight recipients each, that is twenty-four recipient intents, not eight. The database and outbox counts expose the original burst before recipient expansion.

## Worked default trace

At tick 1 the database contains n1, n2, and n3. Tick 2 stages their fan-outs; tick 3 creates twenty-four ready jobs. One worker begins claiming at tick 4. With one successful gateway attempt per tick, acceptances start at tick 5 and receipts at tick 6.

The execution horizon ends at tick 24 before this healthy default fully drains: twenty jobs have gateway acceptance, nineteen distinct receipts exist, and four outstanding jobs remain—three queued and one in flight. The accepted-intent count is twenty-four throughout. Ending playback is not equivalent to finishing the workload.

## Predict, then test

First raise **Worker slots** to four while keeping **Gateway attempts / tick** at one. Predict whether the queue drains sooner. Dispatch is paced at min(worker slots, gateway quota), so only one job is claimed per tick and useful throughput remains unchanged. More concurrency alone cannot exceed downstream capacity.

Now set both worker slots and gateway rate to four under healthy failure settings. Twenty-four jobs fit six dispatch rounds: claims at ticks 4–9, acceptances at 5–10, and all receipts by tick 11. Compare equal snapshots and counters, rather than comparing playback animation speed.

## Defend the production plan

A finite batch demonstrates drain behavior; continuous arrivals, autoscaling, network latency distributions, and shard placement are not simulated. For production, estimate recipient-job arrival rate, sustainable service capacity, and backlog age. Explain why a provider quota caps useful throughput even when compute is abundant. Then discuss per-tenant quotas, token/recipient partition keys, and ordering scopes as design extensions.

The admission-budget control applies only to the backpressure scenario. Changing it here does not change this workload.

[FCM scaling guidance](https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging/scale-fcm) discusses quotas, 429 responses, retry behavior, and traffic smoothing. Use those constraints to justify paced dispatch and headroom, rather than answering every throughput problem with more workers.

## Lab controls
Use the execution player to **step, play, rewind, or scrub ticks 0–24**. Changing a parameter recomputes the entire run from tick 0; it does not inject a new event at the current tick. The failure selector chooses a reproducible failure schedule. Each tick is a simulation scheduling round, not a measured second.

Cells carry logical IDs such as `n1:u1`; the same ID can appear in history and live state. Database and outbox cells are notification IDs, while delivery cells identify notification/recipient pairs. Each recipient has one modeled device. Arrays are projections of records, not a suggested database schema. A `+N more` cell summarizes additional entries; counters retain exact totals. Empty structures show ∅. The amber cell rim indicates an array position changed; it is not a guarantee of animated identity across services.

Commit occurs at tick 1, relay at 2, expansion at 3, worker claim at 4, provider response at 5, and earliest device receipt at 6. Worker slots and gateway attempts per tick independently constrain dispatch. Retry delays are deterministic exponential backoff, capped at three attempts. Failure 4 keeps the provider unavailable through tick 24, exposing retry exhaustion and dead letters. Production needs jitter, Retry-After handling, durable leases, and observability. Device receipt is modeled evidence; display and opening are outside this model.

The dedupe ledger suppresses **known completed replays**; it cannot remove uncertainty after a remote acceptance with a lost acknowledgment. At-most-once refuses retries and can lose work. The bounded at-least-once policy retries transient failures but can end in a dead letter; it does not promise eventual device delivery.


**Records view:** inspect DB → outbox → Kafka intent-events → Flink input → Kafka delivery-jobs → worker consumer backlog → workers → gateway → device, followed by retry, completion, terminal, and deferred state. Kafka topic logs retain records after consumption; the worker backlog shrinks when claims advance the consumer position. Gateway/device histories include repeated attempts; the receipt counter counts distinct recipients.

The dashboard cells are exact counters: Gateway counts acceptance events, Receipts counts distinct modeled recipient receipts, Duplicates counts repeated gateway acceptance, Writes counts the illustrative commit/materialization operations, and Terminal counts permanent failures, exhausted retries, or abandoned uncertain attempts.


## Sender and audience resolution

Each intent carries a notification identity and a sender/source identity. A sender can be a publisher, channel, organization, or user. The follower subscriptions table links a known recipient to a followed source. Fan-out queries that relation, joins the recipient directory, deduplicates targets, and applies the **Follower query limit** before expanding delivery jobs. The source directory and recipient directory are explicit modeled records, not live personal data. Change **Sender / followed source**: publisher-1 has 40 followers, while channel-2 has u2, u4, u6, and u8. A limit of three selects u1/u2/u3 for publisher-1 and u2/u4/u6 for channel-2. The limit never invents a recipient.

The two lookup arrows show query and result, distinct from deferred-work arrows. Lookup is synchronous within the fan-out tick; lookup latency, pagination, subscription changes, privacy rules, and device-token lookup are not simulated. Admission preflights this fixed subscription snapshot to reserve exact target obligations. Production must choose an audience snapshot and handle changes between admission and processing. Deferred readers contains already resolved recipients; it is not the subscription directory. Use Records for source identities, selected subscription links, and resolved request-to-recipient pairs.


## Inspect the scenario data

The data section contains ordinary tables: settings (one row of scalar options), submissions (tick/count rows), sources and targets (identity rows), memberships (source/target rows), replays (tick/request/target rows), and receiptExclusions (target rows). There is no serialized model cell. dataTable(name) supplies a whole table; dataTable(name,row,column) still reads one cell. The domain combines these structured inputs at evaluation time. Edit a subscription row to change who follows a source.
scenes.prompt: Three notifications commit tick1, yielding 24 jobs. Default horizon24 has accepted24 providerAccepted20 delivered19 backlog4, queued3 and worker1. Four workers/rate4 finish receipts11. Workers4/rate1 causes throttling/retries, not linear improvement. Do not promise simulation of sharding or autoscaling. Explain concrete boundaries: Kafka owns retained topic logs; Flink contains KafkaSource, fan-out operator, and KafkaSink. Delivery workers and external APNs/FCM are outside Flink. Use Architecture for ownership and Records for identities. Checkpoints, partitions, and transactional connector guarantees are production discussion, not simulated features. Explain that intents contain sender/source identity, which may identify a channel rather than a user. Followers are selected from explicit subscriptions and a known target directory. The recipients slider is a query limit, not synthetic user creation. Do not claim lookup latency or live user data are modeled.

scenes.title: Retries and Dead Letters
scenes.description: Turn a gateway outage into delayed work, then distinguish recovery from retry amplification.
scenes.markdown:
## Recover without multiplying the outage
A transient failure is a scheduling decision, not permission to spin. The default run commits one notification for four recipients. It claims work at tick 4; responses beginning at tick 5 encounter the injected 429 outage through tick 10. Follow each logical job from in-flight into the delayed-retry array. Its due tick determines when it can return to the ready queue. No recipient job is invented by retrying: attempts change, identity persists.

## Architecture and ownership

The default **Architecture** view shows one concrete deployment. **Blue Kafka** owns two retained topic logs: intent-events and delivery-jobs. **Purple Flink** starts at KafkaSource, expands recipients in the fan-out operator, and ends at KafkaSink. Delivery workers, the retry timer, completion ledger, APNs/FCM, and devices are outside that job. Cylindrical pipes connect named ports across service boundaries; colored pipes mark transitions at the current tick. Nested blocks separate Kafka topic ownership from Flink processing stages. The topic blocks embed existing array objects in their local coordinates. Use **Records** to inspect the actual identities and consumer backlog.

Node status values show notification rows (DB), relayed intents (CDC), retained topic records (Kafka), intents awaiting processing (Flink header), consumed intents (KafkaSource), processing responsibilities (operator/sink), in-flight claims (workers), acceptance/receipt events, or live entries in support stores. The Kafka header marks ownership of both retained logs. Embedded arrays show the first three records; use Records for the full bounded projection. The Dead letters node counts stored permanent failures and exhausted retries. The separate Terminal dashboard also counts abandoned attempts.

Retries publish another delivery record; they do not delete earlier Kafka history. Deferred readers live in a separate read inbox and re-enter fan-out at tick 12. The ledger is checked before sending and records acknowledged completion; a lost provider acknowledgment leaves an uncertain effect.

Flink is a deployment choice for stateful, partitioned fan-out; simpler fan-out workers can implement the same contract. This simulation aggregates topics and consumer positions. It does **not** simulate partitions, checkpoints, consumer crashes, Kafka transactions, or Flink recovery. Kafka-to-Flink-to-Kafka exactly-once processing depends on checkpoint and connector configuration; it does not make a remote APNs/FCM effect exactly once. See [Kafka log and consumer design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/) and [Flink connector guarantees](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/connectors/datastream/guarantees/).

## Follow the current transition

The caption beneath the player explains **this tick**, including which structures changed and why. Use the small execution arrows beside the tick slider to move one scheduling round; the larger lesson arrows move between Predict, Execute, and Defend. Parameter changes recompute the trace from tick 0.

This lab uses deterministic exponential delays, $2^{attempt}$ ticks, and at most three attempts. That makes the trace reproducible; production adds jitter and provider-specific rules. [FCM scaling guidance](https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging/scale-fcm) explains retry amplification and honoring Retry-After. The gateway attempts-per-tick setting is a simplified response quota model, not an exact FCM token bucket or APNs contract. Tick duration is not seconds.

**Experiment:** scrub ticks 4–14 with failure 1, then compare failure 0. Reduce worker slots to one. Does the queue, worker occupancy, or retry due date explain the delay? Next choose failure 3: recipient u1 has an invalid token. Its terminal job belongs in the dead-letter/terminal view; endlessly retrying a permanent failure would waste capacity. [APNs response documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/handling-notification-responses-from-apns) distinguishes inactive tokens and transient responses. A production token registry would retire invalid tokens; that registry mutation is outside this simulation.

Select **Prolonged outage** and advance to tick 13: the first jobs have exhausted their third attempt and enter dead letters. Compare this with the shorter outage, which recovers. Toggle delivery policy to at-most-once. Transient abandonment is counted by the lab's expired metric even though no age-based TTL control exists. Name that loss explicitly. With bounded retries, exhausted work can also terminate; “at least once” here describes a retry strategy, not a guarantee that every device receives a message.

**Staff interview decision:** establish a retry budget, ownership at one layer, deadlines, and priority isolation before increasing concurrency. Ask whether the message is still useful when recovery happens. Discussion extensions include Retry-After, jitter, circuit breakers, a durable due-time index, and controlled dead-letter replay. Those mechanisms are recommendations to defend, not hidden behaviors of this model.

## Lab controls
Use the execution player to **step, play, rewind, or scrub ticks 0–24**. Changing a parameter recomputes the entire run from tick 0; it does not inject a new event at the current tick. The failure selector chooses a reproducible failure schedule. Each tick is a simulation scheduling round, not a measured second.

Cells carry logical IDs such as `n1:u1`; the same ID can appear in history and live state. Database and outbox cells are notification IDs, while delivery cells identify notification/recipient pairs. Each recipient has one modeled device. Arrays are projections of records, not a suggested database schema. A `+N more` cell summarizes additional entries; counters retain exact totals. Empty structures show ∅. The amber cell rim indicates an array position changed; it is not a guarantee of animated identity across services.

Commit occurs at tick 1, relay at 2, expansion at 3, worker claim at 4, provider response at 5, and earliest device receipt at 6. Worker slots and gateway attempts per tick independently constrain dispatch. Retry delays are deterministic exponential backoff, capped at three attempts. Failure 4 keeps the provider unavailable through tick 24, exposing retry exhaustion and dead letters. Production needs jitter, Retry-After handling, durable leases, and observability. Device receipt is modeled evidence; display and opening are outside this model.

The dedupe ledger suppresses **known completed replays**; it cannot remove uncertainty after a remote acceptance with a lost acknowledgment. At-most-once refuses retries and can lose work. The bounded at-least-once policy retries transient failures but can end in a dead letter; it does not promise eventual device delivery.


**Records view:** inspect DB → outbox → Kafka intent-events → Flink input → Kafka delivery-jobs → worker consumer backlog → workers → gateway → device, followed by retry, completion, terminal, and deferred state. Kafka topic logs retain records after consumption; the worker backlog shrinks when claims advance the consumer position. Gateway/device histories include repeated attempts; the receipt counter counts distinct recipients.

The dashboard cells are exact counters: Gateway counts acceptance events, Receipts counts distinct modeled recipient receipts, Duplicates counts repeated gateway acceptance, Writes counts the illustrative commit/materialization operations, and Terminal counts permanent failures, exhausted retries, or abandoned uncertain attempts.


## Sender and audience resolution

Each intent carries a notification identity and a sender/source identity. A sender can be a publisher, channel, organization, or user. The follower subscriptions table links a known recipient to a followed source. Fan-out queries that relation, joins the recipient directory, deduplicates targets, and applies the **Follower query limit** before expanding delivery jobs. The source directory and recipient directory are explicit modeled records, not live personal data. Change **Sender / followed source**: publisher-1 has 40 followers, while channel-2 has u2, u4, u6, and u8. A limit of three selects u1/u2/u3 for publisher-1 and u2/u4/u6 for channel-2. The limit never invents a recipient.

The two lookup arrows show query and result, distinct from deferred-work arrows. Lookup is synchronous within the fan-out tick; lookup latency, pagination, subscription changes, privacy rules, and device-token lookup are not simulated. Admission preflights this fixed subscription snapshot to reserve exact target obligations. Production must choose an audience snapshot and handle changes between admission and processing. Deferred readers contains already resolved recipients; it is not the subscription directory. Use Records for source identities, selected subscription links, and resolved request-to-recipient pairs.


## Inspect the scenario data

The data section contains ordinary tables: settings (one row of scalar options), submissions (tick/count rows), sources and targets (identity rows), memberships (source/target rows), replays (tick/request/target rows), and receiptExclusions (target rows). There is no serialized model cell. dataTable(name) supplies a whole table; dataTable(name,row,column) still reads one cell. The domain combines these structured inputs at evaluation time. Edit a subscription row to change who follows a source.
scenes.prompt: Explain ready versus delayed retry state. Classify permanent and transient errors. Emphasize deterministic delays are teaching simplifications and bounded retries can fail. Ask why gateway capacity and retry budget matter more than unlimited workers. Explain concrete boundaries: Kafka owns retained topic logs; Flink contains KafkaSource, fan-out operator, and KafkaSink. Delivery workers and external APNs/FCM are outside Flink. Use Architecture for ownership and Records for identities. Checkpoints, partitions, and transactional connector guarantees are production discussion, not simulated features. Explain that intents contain sender/source identity, which may identify a channel rather than a user. Followers are selected from explicit subscriptions and a known target directory. The recipients slider is a query limit, not synthetic user creation. Do not claim lookup latency or live user data are modeled.

scenes.title: The Ambiguous Send Window
scenes.description: Separate completed-job replay suppression from uncertainty after remote acceptance.
scenes.markdown:
## One logical job can produce two remote acceptances
At tick 1 the database records n1; expansion creates one job per recipient. The default failure loses the first acceptance acknowledgment: a gateway accepts work, but the worker cannot confidently record success. Trace the same logical ID through history and its retry. The acceptance history and duplicate counter expose repeated external effects even while the local job identity remains stable.

## Architecture and ownership

The default **Architecture** view shows one concrete deployment. **Blue Kafka** owns two retained topic logs: intent-events and delivery-jobs. **Purple Flink** starts at KafkaSource, expands recipients in the fan-out operator, and ends at KafkaSink. Delivery workers, the retry timer, completion ledger, APNs/FCM, and devices are outside that job. Cylindrical pipes connect named ports across service boundaries; colored pipes mark transitions at the current tick. Nested blocks separate Kafka topic ownership from Flink processing stages. The topic blocks embed existing array objects in their local coordinates. Use **Records** to inspect the actual identities and consumer backlog.

Node status values show notification rows (DB), relayed intents (CDC), retained topic records (Kafka), intents awaiting processing (Flink header), consumed intents (KafkaSource), processing responsibilities (operator/sink), in-flight claims (workers), acceptance/receipt events, or live entries in support stores. The Kafka header marks ownership of both retained logs. Embedded arrays show the first three records; use Records for the full bounded projection. The Dead letters node counts stored permanent failures and exhausted retries. The separate Terminal dashboard also counts abandoned attempts.

Retries publish another delivery record; they do not delete earlier Kafka history. Deferred readers live in a separate read inbox and re-enter fan-out at tick 12. The ledger is checked before sending and records acknowledged completion; a lost provider acknowledgment leaves an uncertain effect.

Flink is a deployment choice for stateful, partitioned fan-out; simpler fan-out workers can implement the same contract. This simulation aggregates topics and consumer positions. It does **not** simulate partitions, checkpoints, consumer crashes, Kafka transactions, or Flink recovery. Kafka-to-Flink-to-Kafka exactly-once processing depends on checkpoint and connector configuration; it does not make a remote APNs/FCM effect exactly once. See [Kafka log and consumer design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/) and [Flink connector guarantees](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/connectors/datastream/guarantees/).

## Follow the current transition

The caption beneath the player explains **this tick**, including which structures changed and why. Use the small execution arrows beside the tick slider to move one scheduling round; the larger lesson arrows move between Predict, Execute, and Defend. Parameter changes recompute the trace from tick 0.

The completed-job ledger solves a narrower problem. At tick 12 a replay publisher appends a duplicate record for completed n1:u1 to Kafka delivery-jobs. This models duplicate publication; a consumer crash or offset rewind is not simulated. With dedupe enabled, a **known completed replay** is suppressed. Disable dedupe and compare the final attempt and acceptance counts. Now restore dedupe and inspect the earlier lost acknowledgment. A completed ledger cannot suppress an uncertain result that has not been durably recorded. This distinction is central to [safe idempotent API retries](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/).

**Experiment:** compare failure 0 and failure 2 at ticks 5, 8, 12, and 24. Identify which duplicate comes from uncertain acceptance and which comes from deliberate replay. Keep recipients at four and gateway attempts at two before changing concurrency so the causal comparison is clear. The device history is modeled receipt evidence; repeated acceptance need not mean repeated visible alerts in a real provider or client.

A unique constraint on event, recipient, and channel can make local job creation idempotent. Marking a local record complete before sending risks omission if the process crashes; marking it after sending retains the remote uncertainty window. Durable queue leases also do not guarantee unique processing: [SQS visibility documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html) describes redelivery and duplicate possibilities.

**Staff interview decision:** state exactly which side effect is deduplicated, which key identifies intent, and how long that key survives. Distinguish a logical message ID from an attempt ID. Discussion extensions include atomic local ledger writes, client-side message reconciliation, provider-supported idempotency contracts where available, and retention beyond the replay horizon. None is a claim of end-to-end exactly-once display. Collapse keys replace eligible pending updates under provider rules; they are not general transaction IDs.

## Lab controls
Use the execution player to **step, play, rewind, or scrub ticks 0–24**. Changing a parameter recomputes the entire run from tick 0; it does not inject a new event at the current tick. The failure selector chooses a reproducible failure schedule. Each tick is a simulation scheduling round, not a measured second.

Cells carry logical IDs such as `n1:u1`; the same ID can appear in history and live state. Database and outbox cells are notification IDs, while delivery cells identify notification/recipient pairs. Each recipient has one modeled device. Arrays are projections of records, not a suggested database schema. A `+N more` cell summarizes additional entries; counters retain exact totals. Empty structures show ∅. The amber cell rim indicates an array position changed; it is not a guarantee of animated identity across services.

Commit occurs at tick 1, relay at 2, expansion at 3, worker claim at 4, provider response at 5, and earliest device receipt at 6. Worker slots and gateway attempts per tick independently constrain dispatch. Retry delays are deterministic exponential backoff, capped at three attempts. Failure 4 keeps the provider unavailable through tick 24, exposing retry exhaustion and dead letters. Production needs jitter, Retry-After handling, durable leases, and observability. Device receipt is modeled evidence; display and opening are outside this model.

The dedupe ledger suppresses **known completed replays**; it cannot remove uncertainty after a remote acceptance with a lost acknowledgment. At-most-once refuses retries and can lose work. The bounded at-least-once policy retries transient failures but can end in a dead letter; it does not promise eventual device delivery.


**Records view:** inspect DB → outbox → Kafka intent-events → Flink input → Kafka delivery-jobs → worker consumer backlog → workers → gateway → device, followed by retry, completion, terminal, and deferred state. Kafka topic logs retain records after consumption; the worker backlog shrinks when claims advance the consumer position. Gateway/device histories include repeated attempts; the receipt counter counts distinct recipients.

The dashboard cells are exact counters: Gateway counts acceptance events, Receipts counts distinct modeled recipient receipts, Duplicates counts repeated gateway acceptance, Writes counts the illustrative commit/materialization operations, and Terminal counts permanent failures, exhausted retries, or abandoned uncertain attempts.


## Sender and audience resolution

Each intent carries a notification identity and a sender/source identity. A sender can be a publisher, channel, organization, or user. The follower subscriptions table links a known recipient to a followed source. Fan-out queries that relation, joins the recipient directory, deduplicates targets, and applies the **Follower query limit** before expanding delivery jobs. The source directory and recipient directory are explicit modeled records, not live personal data. Change **Sender / followed source**: publisher-1 has 40 followers, while channel-2 has u2, u4, u6, and u8. A limit of three selects u1/u2/u3 for publisher-1 and u2/u4/u6 for channel-2. The limit never invents a recipient.

The two lookup arrows show query and result, distinct from deferred-work arrows. Lookup is synchronous within the fan-out tick; lookup latency, pagination, subscription changes, privacy rules, and device-token lookup are not simulated. Admission preflights this fixed subscription snapshot to reserve exact target obligations. Production must choose an audience snapshot and handle changes between admission and processing. Deferred readers contains already resolved recipients; it is not the subscription directory. Use Records for source identities, selected subscription links, and resolved request-to-recipient pairs.


## Inspect the scenario data

The data section contains ordinary tables: settings (one row of scalar options), submissions (tick/count rows), sources and targets (identity rows), memberships (source/target rows), replays (tick/request/target rows), and receiptExclusions (target rows). There is no serialized model cell. dataTable(name) supplies a whole table; dataTable(name,row,column) still reads one cell. The domain combines these structured inputs at evaluation time. Edit a subscription row to change who follows a source.
scenes.prompt: Keep known-completed replay at tick12 distinct from lost remote ACK. Never say the ledger ensures exactly-once remote effects. Ask learners to locate the side-effect/ledger crash boundary and define key retention. Explain concrete boundaries: Kafka owns retained topic logs; Flink contains KafkaSource, fan-out operator, and KafkaSink. Delivery workers and external APNs/FCM are outside Flink. Use Architecture for ownership and Records for identities. Checkpoints, partitions, and transactional connector guarantees are production discussion, not simulated features. Explain that intents contain sender/source identity, which may identify a channel rather than a user. Followers are selected from explicit subscriptions and a known target directory. The recipients slider is a query limit, not synthetic user creation. Do not claim lookup latency or live user data are modeled.

scenes.title: Bounded Admission and Backpressure
scenes.description: Keep total outstanding recipient intent within a budget before accepting more work.
scenes.markdown:
## A short ready queue can conceal a large debt
This scenario offers four notifications at ticks 1–4. Each default notification represents four recipient jobs. With admission capacity eight and only one worker and one gateway attempt per tick, the system must reject whole notifications when accepting them would exceed its outstanding-recipient budget. The budget counts accepted but unfinished recipient intents wherever they live: outbox, pending expansion, ready queue, in-flight workers, or delayed retries. It is not a limit on just the visible ready array.

## Architecture and ownership

The default **Architecture** view shows one concrete deployment. **Blue Kafka** owns two retained topic logs: intent-events and delivery-jobs. **Purple Flink** starts at KafkaSource, expands recipients in the fan-out operator, and ends at KafkaSink. Delivery workers, the retry timer, completion ledger, APNs/FCM, and devices are outside that job. Cylindrical pipes connect named ports across service boundaries; colored pipes mark transitions at the current tick. Nested blocks separate Kafka topic ownership from Flink processing stages. The topic blocks embed existing array objects in their local coordinates. Use **Records** to inspect the actual identities and consumer backlog.

Node status values show notification rows (DB), relayed intents (CDC), retained topic records (Kafka), intents awaiting processing (Flink header), consumed intents (KafkaSource), processing responsibilities (operator/sink), in-flight claims (workers), acceptance/receipt events, or live entries in support stores. The Kafka header marks ownership of both retained logs. Embedded arrays show the first three records; use Records for the full bounded projection. The Dead letters node counts stored permanent failures and exhausted retries. The separate Terminal dashboard also counts abandoned attempts.

Retries publish another delivery record; they do not delete earlier Kafka history. Deferred readers live in a separate read inbox and re-enter fan-out at tick 12. The ledger is checked before sending and records acknowledged completion; a lost provider acknowledgment leaves an uncertain effect.

Flink is a deployment choice for stateful, partitioned fan-out; simpler fan-out workers can implement the same contract. This simulation aggregates topics and consumer positions. It does **not** simulate partitions, checkpoints, consumer crashes, Kafka transactions, or Flink recovery. Kafka-to-Flink-to-Kafka exactly-once processing depends on checkpoint and connector configuration; it does not make a remote APNs/FCM effect exactly once. See [Kafka log and consumer design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/) and [Flink connector guarantees](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/connectors/datastream/guarantees/).

## Follow the current transition

The caption beneath the player explains **this tick**, including which structures changed and why. Use the small execution arrows beside the tick slider to move one scheduling round; the larger lesson arrows move between Predict, Execute, and Defend. Parameter changes recompute the trace from tick 0.

At tick 1 n1 commits; at tick 2 n2 fits the budget. Compare ticks 3 and 4 with the accepted and rejected counters. Partial fan-out would leave a confusing contract in which some eligible recipients get a notification that was supposedly rejected. The model therefore admits or rejects each notification as a whole. Rejection occurs before persistence of that notification intent; an API contract would need to explain retryability to its caller.

**Experiment:** raise capacity to sixteen, rewind, and observe the larger obligation. Then raise workers to four while keeping gateway attempts at one. Does completion improve proportionally? Increase the gateway setting independently. Finally inject the 429 outage and watch retries continue consuming admission budget. Moving a job to a delayed queue has not made its obligation disappear.

The gateway rate is a simplified response quota model, not an exact vendor quota. This finite four-notification burst cannot establish a steady-state throughput SLO. It does show why capacity must cover all stages and why more concurrency can fail to relieve a downstream cap. [AWS guidance on limiting queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2022-03-31/framework/rel_mitigate_interaction_failure_fail_fast.html) explains how stale backlog can undo the benefit of asynchronous buffering.

**Staff interview decision:** define the admission unit, maximum age, failure response, and fairness policy. Track oldest outstanding age alongside depth and rejection rate. Discussion extensions include reserved capacity for transactional alerts, per-tenant limits, campaign pacing, expiration, and fair partition scheduling. These are proposed production controls; the simulator has one shared budget and no tenant scheduler. Capacity applies to this admission scenario only.

## Lab controls
Use the execution player to **step, play, rewind, or scrub ticks 0–24**. Changing a parameter recomputes the entire run from tick 0; it does not inject a new event at the current tick. The failure selector chooses a reproducible failure schedule. Each tick is a simulation scheduling round, not a measured second.

Cells carry logical IDs such as `n1:u1`; the same ID can appear in history and live state. Database and outbox cells are notification IDs, while delivery cells identify notification/recipient pairs. Each recipient has one modeled device. Arrays are projections of records, not a suggested database schema. A `+N more` cell summarizes additional entries; counters retain exact totals. Empty structures show ∅. The amber cell rim indicates an array position changed; it is not a guarantee of animated identity across services.

Commit occurs at tick 1, relay at 2, expansion at 3, worker claim at 4, provider response at 5, and earliest device receipt at 6. Worker slots and gateway attempts per tick independently constrain dispatch. Retry delays are deterministic exponential backoff, capped at three attempts. Failure 4 keeps the provider unavailable through tick 24, exposing retry exhaustion and dead letters. Production needs jitter, Retry-After handling, durable leases, and observability. Device receipt is modeled evidence; display and opening are outside this model.

The dedupe ledger suppresses **known completed replays**; it cannot remove uncertainty after a remote acceptance with a lost acknowledgment. At-most-once refuses retries and can lose work. The bounded at-least-once policy retries transient failures but can end in a dead letter; it does not promise eventual device delivery.


**Records view:** inspect DB → outbox → Kafka intent-events → Flink input → Kafka delivery-jobs → worker consumer backlog → workers → gateway → device, followed by retry, completion, terminal, and deferred state. Kafka topic logs retain records after consumption; the worker backlog shrinks when claims advance the consumer position. Gateway/device histories include repeated attempts; the receipt counter counts distinct recipients.

The dashboard cells are exact counters: Gateway counts acceptance events, Receipts counts distinct modeled recipient receipts, Duplicates counts repeated gateway acceptance, Writes counts the illustrative commit/materialization operations, and Terminal counts permanent failures, exhausted retries, or abandoned uncertain attempts.


## Sender and audience resolution

Each intent carries a notification identity and a sender/source identity. A sender can be a publisher, channel, organization, or user. The follower subscriptions table links a known recipient to a followed source. Fan-out queries that relation, joins the recipient directory, deduplicates targets, and applies the **Follower query limit** before expanding delivery jobs. The source directory and recipient directory are explicit modeled records, not live personal data. Change **Sender / followed source**: publisher-1 has 40 followers, while channel-2 has u2, u4, u6, and u8. A limit of three selects u1/u2/u3 for publisher-1 and u2/u4/u6 for channel-2. The limit never invents a recipient.

The two lookup arrows show query and result, distinct from deferred-work arrows. Lookup is synchronous within the fan-out tick; lookup latency, pagination, subscription changes, privacy rules, and device-token lookup are not simulated. Admission preflights this fixed subscription snapshot to reserve exact target obligations. Production must choose an audience snapshot and handle changes between admission and processing. Deferred readers contains already resolved recipients; it is not the subscription directory. Use Records for source identities, selected subscription links, and resolved request-to-recipient pairs.


## Inspect the scenario data

The data section contains ordinary tables: settings (one row of scalar options), submissions (tick/count rows), sources and targets (identity rows), memberships (source/target rows), replays (tick/request/target rows), and receiptExclusions (target rows). There is no serialized model cell. dataTable(name) supplies a whole table; dataTable(name,row,column) still reads one cell. The domain combines these structured inputs at evaluation time. Edit a subscription row to change who follows a source.
scenes.prompt: Admission is whole-notification and counts all outstanding recipient intentions, not ready slots. Ask why delayed retries retain debt. Explicitly state capacity is only used in scenario6 and four offered notifications are not a steady-state load test. Explain concrete boundaries: Kafka owns retained topic logs; Flink contains KafkaSource, fan-out operator, and KafkaSink. Delivery workers and external APNs/FCM are outside Flink. Use Architecture for ownership and Records for identities. Checkpoints, partitions, and transactional connector guarantees are production discussion, not simulated features. Explain that intents contain sender/source identity, which may identify a channel rather than a user. Followers are selected from explicit subscriptions and a known target directory. The recipients slider is a query limit, not synthetic user creation. Do not claim lookup latency or live user data are modeled.
