scenes.title: Defend the Delivery Contract
scenes.description: Defend a complete architecture when acceptance, retries, and device availability diverge.
scenes.markdown:
## State the guarantee at every boundary
A notification service can durably accept intent without promising that a person sees an alert. This capstone deliberately keeps device u1 offline indefinitely. The default also loses the first gateway acceptance acknowledgment. Watch the database, outbox, ready queue, retry structure, completion ledger, gateway history, and device history together. A cleared local backlog and a growing acceptance counter still do not establish receipt for u1.

## Architecture and ownership

The default **Architecture** view shows one concrete deployment. **Blue Kafka** owns two retained topic logs: intent-events and delivery-jobs. **Purple Flink** starts at KafkaSource, expands recipients in the fan-out operator, and ends at KafkaSink. Delivery workers, the retry timer, completion ledger, APNs/FCM, and devices are outside that job. Cylindrical pipes connect named ports across service boundaries; colored pipes mark transitions at the current tick. Nested blocks separate Kafka topic ownership from Flink processing stages. The topic blocks embed existing array objects in their local coordinates. Use **Records** to inspect the actual identities and consumer backlog.

Node status values show notification rows (DB), relayed intents (CDC), retained topic records (Kafka), intents awaiting processing (Flink header), consumed intents (KafkaSource), processing responsibilities (operator/sink), in-flight claims (workers), acceptance/receipt events, or live entries in support stores. The Kafka header marks ownership of both retained logs. Embedded arrays show the first three records; use Records for the full bounded projection. The Dead letters node counts stored permanent failures and exhausted retries. The separate Terminal dashboard also counts abandoned attempts.

Retries publish another delivery record; they do not delete earlier Kafka history. Deferred readers live in a separate read inbox and re-enter fan-out at tick 12. The ledger is checked before sending and records acknowledged completion; a lost provider acknowledgment leaves an uncertain effect.

Flink is a deployment choice for stateful, partitioned fan-out; simpler fan-out workers can implement the same contract. This simulation aggregates topics and consumer positions. It does **not** simulate partitions, checkpoints, consumer crashes, Kafka transactions, or Flink recovery. Kafka-to-Flink-to-Kafka exactly-once processing depends on checkpoint and connector configuration; it does not make a remote APNs/FCM effect exactly once. See [Kafka log and consumer design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/) and [Flink connector guarantees](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/connectors/datastream/guarantees/).

## Follow the current transition

The caption beneath the player explains **this tick**, including which structures changed and why. Use the small execution arrows beside the tick slider to move one scheduling round; the larger lesson arrows move between Predict, Execute, and Defend. Parameter changes recompute the trace from tick 0.

**Experiment:** keep the four-recipient default and compare ticks 5, 12, and 24. Change failure to Healthy. Does u1 now receive? Its independent offline condition persists in this scene. Compare the two policy choices under Lost first acceptance ACK: at-most-once abandons uncertain transient work, while bounded retries can create duplicate acceptances. The lab records transient abandonment as expired, but has no expiration-duration control. Do not describe that counter as a simulated TTL implementation.

[FCM lifespan documentation](https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging/customize-messages/setting-message-lifespan) explicitly distinguishes acceptance from delivery and explains offline storage and expiration. [APNs request documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/sending-notification-requests-to-apns) describes best-effort delivery and possible reordering. Neither provider response alone is a user-visible display acknowledgment. Gateway attempts per tick remain a toy response quota; platform scheduling, radio state, operating-system policies, and actual provider storage are not modeled.

**Staff interview defense:** describe a durable intent contract backed by a transactional outbox, bounded processing attempts, stable recipient-job identity, and measurable completion stages. Name who owns retries and reconciliation. Explain the trade between omissions and duplicate risk when remote outcomes are unknown. For critical information, the persistent application inbox or authoritative state should support reconciliation when the client reconnects; push is a prompt to retrieve state, not the sole durable record.

Discussion extensions include client receipt telemetry, display/open analytics, sequence-aware reconciliation, preference and token changes during delayed fan-out, multi-region ownership, and high-priority isolation. Explicitly distinguish those proposals from the implemented simulation. Conclude with conditional guarantees and failure recovery rather than claiming end-to-end exactly-once delivery. A strong design identifies its blind spots and uses SLOs measured at the relevant boundary.

## Lab controls
Use the execution player to **step, play, rewind, or scrub ticks 0–24**. Changing a parameter recomputes the entire run from tick 0; it does not inject a new event at the current tick. The failure selector chooses a reproducible failure schedule. Each tick is a simulation scheduling round, not a measured second.

Cells carry logical IDs such as `n1:u1`; the same ID can appear in history and live state. Database and outbox cells are notification IDs, while delivery cells identify notification/recipient pairs. Each recipient has one modeled device. Arrays are projections of records, not a suggested database schema. A `+N more` cell summarizes additional entries; counters retain exact totals. Empty structures show ∅. The amber cell rim indicates an array position changed; it is not a guarantee of animated identity across services.

Commit occurs at tick 1, relay at 2, expansion at 3, worker claim at 4, provider response at 5, and earliest device receipt at 6. Worker slots and gateway attempts per tick independently constrain dispatch. Retry delays are deterministic exponential backoff, capped at three attempts. Failure 4 keeps the provider unavailable through tick 24, exposing retry exhaustion and dead letters. Production needs jitter, Retry-After handling, durable leases, and observability. Device receipt is modeled evidence; display and opening are outside this model.

The dedupe ledger suppresses **known completed replays**; it cannot remove uncertainty after a remote acceptance with a lost acknowledgment. At-most-once refuses retries and can lose work. The bounded at-least-once policy retries transient failures but can end in a dead letter; it does not promise eventual device delivery.


**Records view:** inspect DB → outbox → Kafka intent-events → Flink input → Kafka delivery-jobs → worker consumer backlog → workers → gateway → device, followed by retry, completion, terminal, and deferred state. Kafka topic logs retain records after consumption; the worker backlog shrinks when claims advance the consumer position. Gateway/device histories include repeated attempts; the receipt counter counts distinct recipients.

The dashboard cells are exact counters: Gateway counts acceptance events, Receipts counts distinct modeled recipient receipts, Duplicates counts repeated gateway acceptance, Writes counts the illustrative commit/materialization operations, and Terminal counts permanent failures, exhausted retries, or abandoned uncertain attempts.


## Sender and audience resolution

Each intent carries a notification identity and a sender/source identity. A sender can be a publisher, channel, organization, or user. The follower subscriptions table links a known recipient to a followed source. Fan-out queries that relation, joins the recipient directory, deduplicates targets, and applies the **Follower query limit** before expanding delivery jobs. The source directory and recipient directory are explicit modeled records, not live personal data. Change **Sender / followed source**: publisher-1 has 40 followers, while channel-2 has u2, u4, u6, and u8. A limit of three selects u1/u2/u3 for publisher-1 and u2/u4/u6 for channel-2. The limit never invents a recipient.

The two lookup arrows show query and result, distinct from deferred-work arrows. Lookup is synchronous within the fan-out tick; lookup latency, pagination, subscription changes, privacy rules, and device-token lookup are not simulated. Admission preflights this fixed subscription snapshot to reserve exact target obligations. Production must choose an audience snapshot and handle changes between admission and processing. Deferred readers contains already resolved recipients; it is not the subscription directory. Use Records for source identities, selected subscription links, and resolved request-to-recipient pairs.


## Inspect the scenario data

The data section contains ordinary tables: settings (one row of scalar options), submissions (tick/count rows), sources and targets (identity rows), memberships (source/target rows), replays (tick/request/target rows), and receiptExclusions (target rows). There is no serialized model cell. dataTable(name) supplies a whole table; dataTable(name,row,column) still reads one cell. The domain combines these structured inputs at evaluation time. Edit a subscription row to change who follows a source.
scenes.prompt: Capstone u1 remains offline even when failure becomes healthy. Ask learners to distinguish durable intent, provider acceptance, receipt, display, and open. Discuss bounded retry and uncertain result tradeoffs without promising end-to-end exactly-once or eventual receipt. Explain concrete boundaries: Kafka owns retained topic logs; Flink contains KafkaSource, fan-out operator, and KafkaSink. Delivery workers and external APNs/FCM are outside Flink. Use Architecture for ownership and Records for identities. Checkpoints, partitions, and transactional connector guarantees are production discussion, not simulated features. Explain that intents contain sender/source identity, which may identify a channel rather than a user. Followers are selected from explicit subscriptions and a known target directory. The recipients slider is a query limit, not synthetic user creation. Do not claim lookup latency or live user data are modeled.
